sections.sectionText: Interfaces are never neutral. Every menu, health bar, prompt, and button in a game carries politics. They shape not only how players act but what they are invited to think and feel while acting. This course examines game interfaces and user experience through the lens of critical design, treating UI/UX not as a layer of polish applied after the "real" design is done, but as a site where values, arguments, and power relations are built. Drawing on Clark Abt's early framing of serious games as play with purposes beyond entertainment, Ian Bogost's concept of procedural rhetoric (the idea that games persuade through the rules and processes they ask players to enact), and Mary Flanagan's critical play, which treats games as tools for questioning social and cultural norms, we will ask how interface design can reveal, reinforce, or challenge the assumptions embedded in a system. We will pair this with the speculative and critical design tradition of Anthony Dunne and Fiona Raby, who argue that design can provoke reflection rather than simply solve problems, and with game-specific interface scholarship, from Kristine Jørgensen's work on game-world interfaces to Zagal, Björk, and Lewis's analysis of dark patterns that exploit players against their own interests. Throughout the semester, students will analyze existing games, critique conventional usability ideals of "frictionlessness" and "intuitiveness," and design their own interface prototypes that use friction, ambiguity, and discomfort deliberately, as means of making players notice, question, and reflect.

sections.sectionText: This course invites design students to explore the intersection of artificial intelligence, emotion, and storytelling in shaping the next generation of products and services. Students will learn how to design for AI-driven experiences that go beyond technical function, emphasizing emotional resonance and human connection. Through critical engagement with contemporary debates on AI, the course highlights the role of emotional intelligence and narrative in creating empathetic, meaningful, and human-centered AI design solutions. This course is open for enrollment to students from engineering, architecture, and both graduate and undergraduate students at the senior/junior level.

sections.sectionText: Living Between Worlds: Women, Migration and the City Living Between Worlds investigates the city as a space of marginal experiences across time and transnational contexts. This seminar probes open-ended ways of rethinking the urban, mainly by foregrounding the experiences of South Asian women in native and diasporic spaces. We experiment with a mix of learning methods that can register embodied, artistic, and archival forms of knowledge. By centering lived experiences from the periphery, this course asks: How do cities accommodate (and erase) women’s labor, mobility, solidarity, and pleasure as spatial practice? In situating South Asian women as subjects, we build on feminist, anti-racist, and post-colonial critiques of dominant, eurocentric ways of imagining urban space.
